item.title: Gram staining differentiates cells largely through cell-envelope behavior during decolorization
item.content: Gram-positive cells typically retain the crystal-violet–iodine complex after decolorization because of their thick peptidoglycan-rich wall, whereas Gram-negative cells are decolorized and then take up the counterstain.
item.explanationMarkdown:
The decisive step is decolorization.

In the classical sequence:

1. crystal violet stains cells
2. iodine forms a crystal-violet–iodine complex
3. alcohol/acetone decolorizer differentially removes the primary stain complex
4. counterstain colors the decolorized Gram-negative cells

A poor decolorization step can therefore cause false Gram reactions.

cards.prompt: Why do Gram-positive cells usually remain purple after Gram staining while Gram-negative cells become counterstain-colored?
cards.answerGuidance: Explain that the crystal-violet–iodine complex is retained more effectively by the thick Gram-positive peptidoglycan during decolorization, while Gram-negative cells are decolorized and then take up the counterstain.
